items.title: [storyblok-backup] storyblok-backup: Stored path traversal via unsanitized Storyblok component names in backup output
items.summary: Summarystoryblok-backup writes files using unsanitized names for Storyblok components, which are content type or schema definitions. This allows a component name containing path traversal sequences to cause backup files to be written outside the intended backup directory. Anyone with component management access in the source Storyblok space, not server access, can plant a malicious component name that causes arbitrary file writes on the machine of anyone who later runs a backup against that space.DetailsThe writeJson function, which takes a folder, a file name, and content, builds the output file path by directly concatenating the backup directory, the folder, and the file name as strings, with no path sanitization or containment check.For the components resource type specifically, the file name used is the component's own name field, which is free text and editable by anyone with component management access in the Storyblok CMS.Other resource types are not affected by this same issue. Stories and datasources use their numeric IDs as filenames, and assets have their filename derived by splitting on the slash character and taking the last segment, which strips path separators. This issue is scoped specifically to components.Since the component name is stored in Storyblok and only read back later when the backup tool runs, this is a stored, second order vulnerability. The malicious value is planted once, then triggers on every subsequent backup run performed by anyone using this tool against that Storyblok space.PoCStep 1 — plant the malicious component name via Storyblok's Management API:curl -X POST "https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces//components/"   -H "Authorization: "   -H "Content-Type: application/json"   -d '{    "component": {      "name": "../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup",      "schema": {}    }  }'Any Storyblok user with component-management permission in the space (not server access to wherever backups run) can do this through the Storyblok UI just as easily, by naming a new component with this value in the component name field.Step 2 — run storyblok-backup against this space, exactly as a normal user would:npx storyblok-backup   --space    --token    --path ./backup   --types "components"Step 3 — observe the actual file write location:With the malicious component name above, the tool's writeJson() function builds the output path as:  backupDir + "/components" + "/../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup" + ".json"which resolves outside ./backup entirely. Confirm with:  ls -la /tmp/evil-storyblok-backup.jsonThe file exists there, outside the --path ./backup directory that was configured, containing the full JSON definition of the malicious component.Step 4 — for comparison, confirm assets and stories are NOT affected:The same defaultFetch() pattern is used for stories and datasources (fileField: numeric id) and for assets (fileField derived via .split('/').at(-1), which strips any path separators from the value before it reaches writeJson()). Only the components resource type passes a raw, unsanitized user-editable string directly into the file path.ImpactAnyone with the ability to create or rename a component in the source Storyblok space, which is a content management privilege and not server access, can cause the backup tool, when run by someone else, to write files outside the intended backup directory on whatever machine runs the backup. Depending on the path chosen and the permissions of the process running the backup, this could overwrite existing files at attacker chosen locations on the host filesystem.Suggested fix: sanitize the component name before using it as a filename, for example by applying the same last-path-segment treatment already used for assets, or by resolving the final path and verifying it stays within the intended backup directory before writing.Referenceshttps://github.com/webflorist/storyblok-backup/security/advisories/GHSA-vcx7-pfrh-mcfghttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115565https://github.com/webflorist/storyblok-backup/commit/f4e4bb1979832abd7e4eb1666e2b3cfc767f587ahttps://github.com/webflorist/storyblok-backup/releases/tag/v0.7.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcx7-pfrh-mcfg

items.title: [js-toml] js-toml allows uncontrolled recursion in `load()` leading `RangeError` (stack exhaustion) on deeply nested input
items.summary: Summaryload() parses untrusted TOML using a recursive-descent parser (Chevrotain) and arecursive tree-walking interpreter. Neither the parser nor the interpreter enforces amaximum nesting / key depth. A small, attacker-controlled document with deep nesting(arrays, inline tables) or a long dotted key drives recursion past the V8 call-stacklimit, and load() throws an uncaught RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.This is a problem for two reasons:Denial of Service. A tiny payload (≈2 KB) reliably aborts parsing. In anyservice that parses user-supplied TOML, an unhandled RangeError can crash theworker/process (500 / restart loop).Error-contract violation. The library signals invalid input viaSyntaxParseError (see src/load/exception.ts; the entire test suite assertsSyntaxParseError). Consumers that follow this contract —try { load(input); }catch (e) {  if (e instanceof SyntaxParseError) return badRequest();  throw e; // unexpected -> propagates}— will re-throw the RangeError instead of treating the input as malformed,turning malformed input into an unexpected fatal error.ImpactUnauthenticated attacker who can supply a TOML string to an application usingjs-toml can force load() to throw a non-SyntaxParseError error.If the error is not caught by a generic handler, the Node.js process terminates(availability impact).Even when caught generically, the documented/expected error type contract is broken,which can bypass input-validation branches that key off SyntaxParseError.No confidentiality or integrity impact. The error is thrown synchronously and iscatchable, so a consumer that catches all exceptions is not crashed — this is why theseverity is assessed Low–Medium rather than High.Affected code / root causeThere is no depth bound anywhere in the parse pipeline. Recursion occurs in (at least)two independent places:Parser (recursive descent). src/load/parser.ts — array / inlineTablerules recurse through value for each nesting level.Interpreter (tree walk). src/load/interpreter.ts —assignValue, createTable, getOrCreateArray recurse per dotted-key segment, andcleanInternalProperties recurses per object depth.Because there is no configurable or hard limit, the recursion depth is bounded only bythe V8 stack, and overflow surfaces as a raw RangeError.Steps to reproduce (PoC)Environment used: Node.js v20, js-toml@1.1.2.import { load, SyntaxParseError } from 'js-toml';function probe(label, toml) {  try {    load(toml);    console.log(`[OK]            ${label}`);  } catch (e) {    const expected = e instanceof SyntaxParseError;    console.log(`[${e.constructor.name}${expected ? '' : ' (UNEXPECTED)'}] ${label}: ${String(e.message).split('\n')[0]}`);  }}// 1) Deeply nested arrays  (~2 KB payload)probe('nested array depth 1000', 'x = ' + '['.repeat(1000) + ']'.repeat(1000));// 2) Deeply nested inline tableslet v = '1';for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) v = `{ a = ${v} }`;probe('nested inline table depth 1000', 'x = ' + v);// 3) Deep dotted key (interpreter recursion)const key = Array.from({ length: 5000 }, (_, i) => 'a' + i).join('.');probe('dotted key depth 5000', `${key} = 1`);Observed output[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] nested array depth 1000: Maximum call stack size exceeded[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] nested inline table depth 1000: Maximum call stack size exceeded[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] dotted key depth 5000: Maximum call stack size exceededEach case throws RangeError, not SyntaxParseError. Overflow occurs in single-digitmilliseconds, so it is not a CPU-exhaustion issue — it is an immediate, deterministic abort.Notes on thresholds (machine-dependent; exact numbers vary by stack size):Nested arrays / inline tables overflow at roughly depth ~1000 (parser recursion).Dotted keys overflow at roughly depth ~5000 (interpreter recursion); depth 1000 still succeeds.Suggested remediationEnforce an explicit, documented maximum nesting/key depth and surface violations asSyntaxParseError (consistent with all other invalid-input handling). For example:Track current depth in the parser/interpreter and throw SyntaxParseError(e.g. "Maximum nesting depth exceeded") once a configurable limit (e.g. 100–1000)is reached, before the native stack overflows.As a defensive backstop, wrap the top-level load() body so that a thrownRangeError from stack exhaustion is converted into a SyntaxParseError, guaranteeingthe documented error contract holds for all malformed input.A configurable limit (with a safe default) is preferable so legitimate deep documents canopt into a higher bound.DisclosureReported privately via GitHub Security Advisory. Happy to provide additional reproducersor test against a candidate patch.Referenceshttps://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/security/advisories/GHSA-3g82-77xr-68x5https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63386https://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/commit/4e10acf1f99ff3cb443c58b8f0a57664e41e87c6https://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/releases/tag/v1.1.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g82-77xr-68x5

items.title: [@appium/storage-plugin] appium allows unauthenticated arbitrary file/directory deletion in @appium/storage-plugin
items.summary: SummaryThe Appium storage plugin exposes an HTTP endpoint POST /storage/delete that takes a user-supplied name and deletes it from the server storage folder. The handler passes name straight into path.join(storageRoot, name) and then fs.rimraf() without any path sanitization. By sending a name containing ../ sequences, an unauthenticated remote client can escape the storage root and recursively delete arbitrary files and directories that the Appium process user can write, anywhere on the host filesystem.The same plugin's upload path validates the name via fs.sanitizeName (requireValidItemOptions), but the delete path does not an asymmetry that makes the missing validation unambiguous.DetailsPublished build (node_modules/@appium/storage-plugin/build/lib/storage.js), and source (packages/storage-plugin/lib/):packages/storage-plugin/lib/storage.ts:65-75 — Storage.delete():async delete(name: string): Promise<boolean> {  if (name.toLowerCase().endsWith(TMP_EXT)) {    return false;  }  const destinationPath = path.join(this._root, name);   // <-- no sanitization  if (!(await fs.exists(destinationPath))) {    return false;  }  await fs.rimraf(destinationPath);                       // <-- recursive delete  return true;}packages/storage-plugin/lib/plugin.ts:77-83 — handler passes raw body:STORAGE_HANDLERS.deleteStorageItem = async function deleteStorageItem(req) {  return await executeStorageMethod(    async (storage) => await storage.delete(parseRequestArgs(req, ['name']).name),  );};parseRequestArgs (plugin.ts:94-106) only checks that the key exists; it does not validate the value.Contrast — the upload path does sanitize: storage.ts:53-54 add() →requireValidItemOptions() (storage.ts:236-256) rejects any name that differs from fs.sanitizeName(name). delete() skips this entirely.PoCInstall and start the server with the storage plugin:npm install appium@3.5.0./node_modules/.bin/appium plugin install --source=npm @appium/storage-plugin./node_modules/.bin/appium --use-plugins=storage --address 127.0.0.1 --port 4723(Default --address is 0.0.0.0; 127.0.0.1 used here for a contained test.)Plant a victim file/dir outside the storage root, then delete via traversal:mkdir -p /tmp/pv_dir && echo SECRET > /tmp/pv_dir/important.txtecho single > /tmp/pv_file.txtcurl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4723/storage/delete \  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  -d '{"name":"../../../../../../../../../../tmp/pv_file.txt"}'# -> {"value":true}curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4723/storage/delete \  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  -d '{"name":"../../../../../../../../../../tmp/pv_dir"}'# -> {"value":true}ImpactAn unauthenticated attacker who can reach the Appium HTTP port (network by default, or cross-origin via a victim browser due to default CORS + no auth) can recursively delete any file or directory writable by the Appium process user. On CI runners, device farms, and developer machines this enables destruction of source trees, build artifacts, SSH keys, configuration, or the OS user profile data loss and denial of service. Appium frequently runs with broad privileges on shared device-lab hosts, amplifying impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/appium/appium/security/advisories/GHSA-jwgx-mp9m-jwcrhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58192https://github.com/appium/appium/pull/22362https://github.com/appium/appium/commit/5fee01752f2782e96fbe64fd13520b433d4a7535https://github.com/appium/appium/releases/tag/%40appium/storage-plugin%401.1.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwgx-mp9m-jwcr
